rv.q: Affection is the key that opens the show's comedy: You feel for Doug and Bud, and even root for them.
The only trigger warning required is one that cautions laughter ahead.
At first, all off the goings-on are entertaining in a crazy kind of way — until they become less and less so.
For the most part—thanks to its completely winning stars, and to the play’s own best stretches of joyful buffoonery—yes.
With all of this pseudo-historical absurdity, Brown and King’s dotty comedy ultimately grounds itself in the likeability of its frontmen: Gad and Rannells.
But it’s not a 100% laugh riot either.

Still, even at a fairly pacey two hours the fun eventually turns to wheel-spinning, since the central gag—the ludicrous mismatch between content and form—is established from the start and then merely elaborated.
Here the problem is not excess but triteness; the tropes of sincere incompetence and pathetic ambition are too familiar, if expertly carried out.
Gad and Rannells are simply divine delivering a master class in musical comedy and likely setting a land/speed record for laughs per minute.

Thanks to these stars, if you head to the James Theater, you’ll laugh. You’ll wince. You may even tear up a bit. Above all, you’ll be incredibly impressed by the pair’s incredible chemistry as well as their go-for-broke mentality in selling this ridiculous material. Without question, Gad and Rannells absolutely earn an A+ for effort.
If you feel the need to laugh and let go, you can trust Andrew Rannells and Josh Gad, formerly stars of The Book of Mormon, to be your expert facilitators.
What makes it worth the visit is the time we get to spend with Bud and Doug.
I would have happily sat twice as long as that through a production of this quality.
The humor in Gutenberg! could stand to be a bit more like the rat-infested streets upon which the meta-show’s characters walk, and a certain nastiness could have elevated this from good to great.
Somehow the comedy gets drained during these asides and the show comes to a stop.
The show is a roughly 2-hour sketch – one that’s clever and filled with laughs but too long and overstuffed to ward off diminishing returns.
In fact, there’s a bit of genius in their stupidity.

The problem is that the show they’ve supposedly devised is not particularly funny, with the relatively esoteric subject matter not exactly lending itself to riotous satire – even Mel Brooks would have trouble coming up with more than a few throwaway gags about Gutenberg.
There are some funny lines, but no more than an hour’s worth of laughs in a two-person vaudeville routine that goes on for two hours, becoming tedious.
It manages to waste the talent of not one but two very talented performers.
Gutenberg!, nimbly directed by Alex Timbers, is a blast from beginning to end.
Skillfully directed by Alex Timbers, “Gutenberg” is absurd, so don’t come for the story or expect to learn anything.
It’s difficult to watch performers work this hard when the humor isn’t exactly there in the source material.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this deliberately silly two-hander, with some finding Gad and Rannells' chemistry effortlessly hilarious while others feel the thin premise stretches an hour of jokes across two tedious hours.

vr.q: that's where I think this two or three star material gets elevated into a four-star evening at the theater because they're both so wonderful in it
I did get a little tired of it after a while... I think I wanted more for the show to reach that next level comedy status, but I still found it super clever and enjoyable.
